source: Auer, Cesa-Bianchi, Fischer (2002) Finite-time analysis of the multiarmed bandit problem
finding: UCB1 picks the arm with the highest average reward plus a confidence bonus sqrt(2 ln t / s). It has logarithmic regret uniformly over time, not only in the limit. This is the bandit rule UCT puts in every tree node.
numbers: Theorem 1: expected pulls of a suboptimal arm j are at most 8 ln n / Delta_j^2 plus a constant, for rewards in [0,1], K>1 arms, any n.
quote: Sketch of the deterministic policy UCB1
limits: Needs i.i.d. rewards per arm. In a search tree the rewards below a node drift, so the theorem does not apply directly (fixed by the UCT paper).
agent_relevance: The explore/exploit bonus is a rule a program can compute from counts. No model judgement needed (fits G1: act on counts).

source: Auer, Cesa-Bianchi, Fischer (2002) Finite-time analysis of the multiarmed bandit problem
finding: Variants were compared on 8 reward distributions. UCB1-TUNED (variance-aware bound) did best in nearly all cases. Epsilon-greedy was good only when its constant c was tuned, and degraded quickly when it was not.
numbers: Experiments over distributions 1-14 (2, 3, 5, 10 arms); UCB1-TUNED best on essentially all; epsilon-greedy near-best only with the empirically best c.
limits: The tuned variant has no proof. The 8 ln n / Delta^2 bound is loose in practice.
agent_relevance: Exploration constants matter a lot. Treat any fixed c in the scaffold as a tunable, not a truth.

source: Kocsis and Szepesvari (2006) Bandit based Monte-Carlo planning
finding: UCT applies UCB1 at every internal node of a lookahead tree built from random-rollout episodes. Node values are averages of rollout returns. Because the payoff below a node drifts as the tree grows, the bias must be c = 2*Cp*sqrt(ln t / s) with a constant Cp chosen so drift conditions hold.
numbers: Theorem 1 generalises UCB1: E[T_i(n)] <= 16 Cp^2 ln n/(Delta_i/2)^2 + 2 N0 + pi^2/3, for drifting payoffs. Lower bound Theorem 3: pulls of any arm >= rho*log(n).
quote: bias terms of the form c = 2Cp sqrt(ln t / s)
limits: Analysis assumes drift conditions on lower levels; N0 can be huge. The paper claims consistency, not fast rates.
agent_relevance: Defines select, expand, simulate, back up with one counted rule. This is the core control loop we could copy.

source: Kocsis and Szepesvari (2006) Bandit based Monte-Carlo planning
finding: Consistency proof: the probability of choosing a non-optimal action at the root goes to zero as samples grow. Bias of the root value estimate is O(log(n)/n) when bias terms are scaled by tree depth D.
numbers: Theorem 5: failure probability at root <= C (1/t)^(rho * (min_i Delta_i/2)^2) for some constant C. Theorem 4 is a concentration bound with deviation delta_n = 9*sqrt(2 n ln(2/eps)).
limits: Rates depend on the minimum gap Delta. Guarantee is asymptotic; later work showed the worst case is far worse (see a12).
agent_relevance: For a small LLM budget (tens of rollouts) the guarantee says little. Use it as design motivation only.

source: Kocsis and Szepesvari (2006) Bandit based Monte-Carlo planning
finding: P-game experiment: random minimax trees where move values come from [0,127] for MAX and [-127,0] for MIN, win decided by sign of summed values. UCT reached low failure rates in about the same number of leaf visits as alpha-beta, order B^(D/2). Plain Monte Carlo (MC) plateaued at a high failure rate, and minimax-updated MC (MMMC) was worse than MC.
numbers: Figure 2: branching B=2, depth D=20 and a second setting; 95% CIs shown for UCT. Figure 3: iterations to reach a failure level scale about B^(D/2) on log-log axes; at higher allowed failure UCT is faster.
limits: Synthetic trees only, one reward model. Go-like structure is argued, not tested here.
agent_relevance: Selection by confidence bound beats uniform sampling at equal budget: steer sampling, do not spread it evenly.

source: Kocsis and Szepesvari (2006) Bandit based Monte-Carlo planning
finding: Sailing domain (stochastic shortest path, 24 x grid-size states): UCT needed far fewer simulator samples than ARTDP and PG-ID for error under 0.1, and scaled better with problem size.
numbers: Grid sizes 2x2 to 40x40; target error < 0.1; samples counted as simulator calls (Figure 4).
limits: One MDP, error measured against known optimum; no seed variance in text.
agent_relevance: Selective tree growth beats full lookahead as problems grow. Supports budgeted selective expansion.

source: Coulom (2006) Efficient selectivity and backup operators in Monte-Carlo tree search
finding: Introduced the name Monte-Carlo tree search, in the Go program Crazy Stone. It selects moves by an estimated probability of being best (Gaussian-based selectivity) and backs up with an operator between mean and max that moves toward max as visits grow. Crazy Stone won the 9x9 Go tournament at the 2006 Computer Olympiad (from memory).
numbers: Not opened this session; no figures recorded.
limits: Not verified from the text.
agent_relevance: Same select/backup design found independently of UCT. The mean-to-max backup is an alternative to pure averaging.

source: Chaslot, Winands, van den Herik, Uiterwijk, Bouzy (2008) Progressive strategies for Monte-Carlo tree search
finding: Added domain knowledge to UCT without slowing it. Progressive bias adds f(n)=H_i/(n_i+1) to the UCT score so the prior dominates early and fades with visits. Progressive unpruning starts with few children and adds more as visits grow. In Go program Mango both together raised the 9x9 win rate against GNU Go from 33.2% to 61.7%.
numbers: 9x9, 20,000 simulations/move, GNU Go level 10: none 33.2% (1000 games), PB 37.2%, PU 58.3%, PB+PU 61.7% (2000 games). 13x13: 8.5%, 15.6%, 30.0%, 35.1% (500 games each).
limits: Heuristic H came from patterns learned on 2,000 professional games (89,119 patterns). One opponent program. Column-to-value alignment read from a table extracted from PDF.
agent_relevance: A prior from a cheap model steers early search and fades out. Same shape as the PUCT prior and as an LLM proposal prior.

source: Chaslot et al. (2008) Progressive strategies for MCTS (19x19 result)
finding: On 19x19, plain MCTS could not beat GNU Go level 0. Only the combination of both progressive strategies reached near parity.
numbers: 19x19, 20,000 sims, GNU Go level 0: none 0% (200 games), PB 3.1%, PU 4.8%, PB+PU 48.2% (500 games).
limits: Gain is super-additive: each strategy alone gives little. Level 0 is the weakest GNU Go setting.
agent_relevance: In wide branching spaces unguided search fails. Guidance plus gradual widening can turn failure into parity. Relevant to wide LLM action spaces.

source: Gelly and Silver (2011) Monte-Carlo tree search and rapid action value estimation in computer Go
finding: RAVE estimates a move's value also from all simulations where that move appeared later in the sequence, blended with the usual UCT value. It speeds learning in early visits. Not opened (download failed).
numbers: Not opened; no figures recorded.
limits: Assumes a move's value is similar across contexts: true in Go, false in many domains.
agent_relevance: Sharing statistics across similar nodes cuts cost. For LLM thoughts this needs a similarity rule, which is risky.

source: Browne et al. (2012) A survey of Monte Carlo tree search methods
finding: Standard survey: four phases, many variants (UCT, RAVE, progressive widening, parallelisation) and applications. Not opened this session (host unreachable).
numbers: Not opened; no figures recorded.
limits: None verified.
agent_relevance: Use as the map of variants when choosing which MCTS pieces to put in the scaffold.

source: Coquelin and Munos (2007) Bandit algorithms for tree search
finding: Reported that UCT can have worst-case regret that is hyper-exponential in depth on deceptive trees, and proposed a modified bound (BAST). Recorded from memory, not opened.
numbers: Not opened; claim is order of a tower of exponentials in depth D.
limits: Unverified in this session; check before citing the exact form.
agent_relevance: UCT can sink huge budget into a misleading branch. A budget cap and restart rule are needed.

source: Silver et al. (2016) Mastering the game of Go with deep neural networks and tree search
finding: AlphaGo combined MCTS with a policy network as prior and a value network plus rollouts. It beat European champion Fan Hui 5-0. Recorded from memory, not opened.
numbers: Not opened. 5-0 vs Fan Hui.
limits: Needed human game data plus self-play and large compute.
agent_relevance: MCTS gets its power when a learned prior and value replace random rollouts. The LLM would be the prior and value source.

source: Silver et al. (2018) A general RL algorithm that masters chess, shogi and Go through self-play (AlphaZero)
finding: AlphaZero uses MCTS with a network prior and value, no rollouts and no human data. In 100-game matches at one minute per move it lost 0 games to Stockfish and 8 to Elmo. It searched far fewer positions per second than alpha-beta, but its MCTS scaled better with thinking time.
numbers: Chess vs Stockfish: as White 25 W, 25 D, 0 L; as Black 3 W, 47 D, 0 L. Shogi vs Elmo: 43-2-5 as first player, 47-0-3 as second. Go vs 3-day AlphaGo Zero: 31 W/19 L and 29 W/21 L. Search speed 80 thousand positions/s (chess), 40 thousand (shogi) vs 70 million (Stockfish), 35 million (Elmo). 800 simulations per move in training.
quote: AlphaZero searches just 80 thousand positions per second in chess and 40 thousand in shogi
limits: Hardware and time controls were disputed by outside engine experts. Table columns read from PDF text.
agent_relevance: Few well-chosen evaluations beat many blind ones. Argues for selective search over wide sampling.

source: Silver et al. (2018) AlphaZero training speed and noise
finding: Time to pass strong opponents in self-play: Stockfish in 4 hours (300k steps), Elmo in under 2 hours (110k steps), AlphaGo Lee in 8 hours (165k steps). Root exploration used Dirichlet noise and visit-proportional move choice in training.
numbers: Chess 4 h / 300k steps; shogi <2 h / 110k; Go 8 h / 165k; 700,000 steps total, 5,000 first-gen TPUs for self-play.
limits: Compute is thousands of TPUs; wall-clock figures assume parallel self-play.
agent_relevance: Root noise is a cheap exploration device a program can add without model judgement.

source: Schrittwieser et al. (2020) Mastering Atari, Go, chess and shogi by planning with a learned model (MuZero)
finding: MuZero runs MCTS inside a learned model, with no rules given. It matched AlphaZero in Go, chess and shogi and set a new state of the art on 57 Atari games. A learned model supported searches much deeper than those used in training.
numbers: Search: 800 simulations (boards), 50 (Atari). Atari: beat R2D2 on 42 of 57 games, SimPLe on all; MuZero Reanalyze 731% median human-normalised vs 192% IMPALA, 231% Rainbow, 431% LASER at 200M frames. Go: matched perfect-model search up to 10 s thinking vs about 0.1 s in training.
quote: performance improved slightly with search time, but plateaued at around 100 simulations
limits: In Atari the planning gain was small: performance plateaued near 100 simulations, and one simulation (policy only) still did well.
agent_relevance: Search helps less when the model is inaccurate. Put a ceiling on useful budget.

source: Schrittwieser et al. (2020) MuZero ablations: search in training
finding: Training with search beat a matched model-free Q-learning variant on Ms. Pacman. Even 6 simulations per move (fewer than the action count) learned an effective policy, and more simulations jumped higher.
numbers: Ms. Pacman, Figure 3C/3D: model-free variant matched R2D2 but learned slower and ended lower.
limits: One game for the ablations; no confidence intervals in the text.
agent_relevance: Even a tiny search budget gives a better learning signal than a single sample. Supports search as a filter for training data.

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with language model is planning with world model (RAP)
finding: RAP makes the LLM both world model (predict next state) and agent, and runs MCTS over reasoning steps with UCT-style selection and rewards from likelihood, self-evaluation and confidence. On Blocksworld with LLaMA-33B it beat CoT at every plan length.
numbers: Blocksworld success: CoT 0.17 / 0.02 / 0.00 (2/4/6-step); CoT pass@10 0.23/0.07/0.00; CoT with GPT-4 0.50/0.63/0.40; RAP(10) 1.00/0.86/0.26; RAP(20) 1.00/0.88/0.42. RAP average 64%, a 33% relative gain over GPT-4 CoT.
quote: RAP substantially improves over CoT by nearly solving all problems within 4 steps
limits: Small test sets per length. Compute is not matched: RAP(20) uses 20 iterations vs 1 chain.
agent_relevance: Search with an explicit state model beats one chain on long plans. Compute is not matched, so read superiority claims with care.

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with language model is planning with world model (RAP)
finding: On GSM8K RAP with one trace chosen by reward reached 48.8% (LLaMA-33B), above CoT and Least-to-Most with self-consistency. Aggregating across the tree added about 3 points. On ProntoQA RAP reached 94.2% answer and 78.8% proof accuracy.
numbers: GSM8K: CoT 29.4, CoT+SC(10) 46.8, RAP 48.8 (one trace), about +3 with aggregation. ProntoQA: CoT 87.8 answer / 64.8 proof, CoT+SC 89.8, RAP 94.2 / 78.8 (20 iterations vs 20 samples).
limits: Gain over self-consistency on GSM8K is only about 2 points (48.8 vs 46.8). Other GSM8K table cells were garbled in extraction and are not recorded.
agent_relevance: On arithmetic, search beats voting only slightly. Sampling plus checking may match tree search at lower complexity (G4: samples are not independent).

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with language model is planning with world model (RAP)
finding: Full Blocksworld (602 cases) with Llama-2 70B grouped by minimum steps. RAP(10) is far above CoT in Easy and Hard settings and keeps success at 6+ steps while CoT collapses.
numbers: Overall: Easy CoT 0.08 vs RAP(10) 0.65; Hard CoT 0.05 vs RAP(10) 0.51. Easy RAP(10) by steps 2,4,6,8,10: 1.00, 0.99, 0.75, 0.61, 0.32 (as read from extraction).
limits: Reward ablation: action-likelihood reward is vital for planning but not helpful for math, so reward design is task-specific.
agent_relevance: The reward is the weak point of LLM-MCTS. A cheap, task-matched, code-checkable reward is worth more than a clever search rule.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Language Agent Tree Search unifies reasoning, acting, and planning (LATS)
finding: LATS uses MCTS with UCT, an LLM value function with self-consistency, environment feedback and self-reflection. On HotPotQA with GPT-3.5 it beat ToT, RAP and Reflexion at the same trajectory count.
numbers: HotPotQA EM (n=5, k=50): reasoning only: Base 0.32, CoT 0.34, CoT-SC 0.38, ToT 0.55, RAP 0.60, LATS(CoT) 0.62. Acting: ReAct 0.32, ReAct best-of-k 0.38, Reflexion 0.51, ToT(ReAct) 0.39, RAP(ReAct) 0.54, LATS(ReAct) 0.63, LATS(n=10) 0.65, LATS(CoT+ReAct) 0.71.
limits: Gain over RAP is about 2-9 points; baselines are re-implementations. Needs a resettable environment (authors' stated limitation).
agent_relevance: MCTS plus real environment feedback gives a modest edge over simpler tree search, if the state can be reset.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Language Agent Tree Search unifies reasoning, acting, and planning (LATS)
finding: Code generation: LATS reached 92.7% pass@1 on HumanEval with GPT-4 and 83.8% with GPT-3.5; on MBPP (GPT-3.5) 81.1%.
numbers: HumanEval GPT-3.5: CoT 46.9, ReAct 56.9, Reflexion 68.1, ToT 54.4, RAP 63.1, LATS 83.8. GPT-4: base 80.1, Reflexion 91.0, LATS 92.7. MBPP GPT-3.5: CoT 54.9, ReAct 67.0, Reflexion 70.0, ToT 65.8, RAP 71.4, LATS 81.1. 5 solutions per expansion, 8 iterations.
limits: Uses model-generated tests (4) as feedback; real test suite only for final pass@1. With GPT-4 the gain over Reflexion is 1.7 points.
agent_relevance: Where an executable check exists, tree search over code attempts works. Matches G2/G3: real output feeds revision.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Language Agent Tree Search unifies reasoning, acting, and planning (LATS)
finding: Ablations on HotPotQA (GPT-3.5): replacing MCTS selection and backup with DFS plus LM pruning costs 0.21; removing the LM heuristic drops to 0.37; removing reflection drops to 0.58 from 0.63.
numbers: LATS(ReAct) 0.63; no LM heuristic 0.37; DFS 0.42; no reflection 0.58. At k=50, ToT 0.49, RAP 0.54, LATS 0.61 (Table 10) or 0.63 (Table 9).
limits: Paper is internally inconsistent: LATS k=50 is 0.63 in one table and 0.61 in another. Node-count columns were garbled in extraction and are not recorded.
agent_relevance: The value function carries most of the gain. Bad values make tree search worse than best-of-k, so validate the value source.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Language Agent Tree Search unifies reasoning, acting, and planning (LATS)
finding: WebShop: LATS improved over ReAct and Reflexion but stayed below human experts and fine-tuned agents. Game of 24: LATS(CoT) 0.44 vs RAP 0.40.
numbers: WebShop score/SR: ReAct best-of-k 59.1/32.0 (k=30), Reflexion 64.2/35.0, LATS 75.9/38.0; IL+RL 62.4/28.7 or 67.5/45.0 and expert 82.1/59.6 (rows partly mis-aligned in extraction). Game of 24: Reflexion 0.12, ToT 0.20, RAP 0.40, LATS(CoT) 0.44.
limits: Authors note generated reflections were often generic and agents got stuck in local minima on WebShop. Row alignment uncertain.
agent_relevance: Generic self-reflection gives little in open tasks. Search helps; unprompted doubt does not (supports G1).

source: Qi et al. (2024) Mutual reasoning makes smaller LLMs stronger problem-solvers (rStar)
finding: rStar runs MCTS with five human-like actions (propose a step, propose the rest, sub-question, re-answer, rephrase), 32 rollouts, then a second small model checks each trajectory by completing it from a partial prefix. Large gains for small models on GSM8K.
numbers: GSM8K: LLaMA2-7B 12.51% to 63.91%; Mistral-7B 36.46% to 81.88%; LLaMA3-8B-Instruct 74.53% to 91.13%. 32 rollouts, depth 5 (8 for MATH).
limits: Baselines are CoT, low for 7B models. Cost: 166.81 model calls and 367.1k tokens per GSM8K question (LLaMA2-7B); full test set took about 4.5 days on one A100 per model.
agent_relevance: Search plus an independent verifier from another model lifts weak models a lot, at about 150 calls per question.

source: Qi et al. (2024) Mutual reasoning makes smaller LLMs stronger problem-solvers (rStar)
finding: Ablations: richer action space helped step by step. RAP-style single-action MCTS saturated after about 4 rollouts and even declined, while rStar and self-consistency kept improving.
numbers: Action space on 200 GSM8K questions, LLaMA3-8B: A3 (RAP) 70.5; +A5 72.5; +A4 73.5; A2+A3+A4+A5 74.0; all five 75.0. Fig. 5: rStar clearly better already at 2 rollouts.
quote: RAP tends to saturate and even decline after 4 rollouts on LLaMA3-8B-Instruct
limits: Steps of 1-2 points on 200 questions are within noise (about plus or minus 3 points). Self-rewarding at intermediate nodes was dropped because small models were unreliable at it.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a small model to score its own steps. Use diverse operators (restate, decompose) plus an independent check. Matches G4.

source: Chen et al. (2024) AlphaMath Almost Zero: process supervision without process
finding: AlphaMath uses MCTS with a value head and PUCT-style selection to create step-level training data from only final-answer correctness. At inference a step-level beam search guided by the value model beat greedy and was proposed because full MCTS inference is too slow.
numbers: DeepSeekMath-Base 7B, first two accuracy columns (assumed GSM8K, MATH): 2-shot prompt 59.7 / 33.2; AlphaMath greedy (K=3) 73.5 / 53.6; + SBS (B1=1) 81.1 / 62.8; + SBS (B1=3) 84.1 / 66.3.
quote: MCTS is computationally intensive for simulations, making it less viable for use in production environments
limits: Column names not verified in the extraction. Needs trained value model and training on labelled answers.
agent_relevance: MCTS is most useful as a teacher and data generator. At run time a cheap value-guided beam may do as well; for a no-training scaffold only the run-time part applies.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) ReST-MCTS*: LLM self-training via process reward guided tree search
finding: ReST-MCTS* infers per-step values from whether a step leads to the known correct answer, guides tree search with them, and keeps good traces for self-training. Under the same sampling budget tree search beat Best-of-N and self-consistency on MATH and SciBench (per paper text).
numbers: Self-training (MATH / GPQA-Diamond / CEval-Hard), LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct: zero-shot 20.76 / 27.27 / 26.32; ReST-MCTS 2nd iteration 34.28 / 27.78 / 25.00 vs ReSTEM 33.52 / 25.25 / 21.71 and Self-Rewarding 33.89 / 26.26 / 23.03. Verifier (256 outputs, Mistral-7B MetaMATH): GSM8K SC 83.9 vs SC+ReST-MCTS value 87.5; MATH500 35.1 vs 39.0.
limits: Gains over ReSTEM and Self-Rewarding are small or flat on GPQA and CEval-Hard; needs ground-truth answers for training.
agent_relevance: Verifier-guided search beats voting by 3-4 points when a trained value model exists. Without one the edge shrinks.

source: Synthesis across opened sources (founding line Auer 2002, Kocsis 2006, Chaslot 2008, Silver 2018, LLM tree search 2023-24)
finding: Three ingredients recur: a counted confidence-bound selection rule, a prior or value from something learned (patterns, networks, an LLM) in place of blind rollouts, and a ceiling on useful budget. LLM versions gain most where a real check exists (code tests, plan validity, known answers) and least where the reward is the model's own opinion.
numbers: Mango 0% to 48.2% on 19x19 only with both prior-based strategies; MuZero Atari plateau near 100 simulations; RAP GSM8K 48.8 vs SC(10) 46.8; LATS DFS-with-pruning 0.42 vs MCTS 0.63; rStar-ablated RAP-style MCTS saturates after about 4 rollouts.
limits: This is the agent's own reading of the sources above, not a new measurement.
agent_relevance: Schema hint: a small tree over operators with counted UCB selection and code-checked leaf values is defensible; self-rated values and generic reflection are not (G1, G2, G3).
